blogs.title: Objective Purpose After Warhol: The Second Circuit Calls Kimmel’s Cameos Transformative Commentary
blogs.description: This post unpacks the court’s first-factor fair use analysis, emphasizing the Supreme Court’s Warhol directive to assess purpose through a reasonable observer rather than subjective intent. It explains why Kimmel’s segments were transformative commentary on Santos’s willingness to “say absurd things for money,” even though Kimmel scripted the prompts, and why alleged deception did not negate fair use in light of Harper & Row’s diminished bad-faith gloss. It also touches on the market-harm framing from Campbell and Hachette—criticism isn’t a licensable substitute—and situates the ruling within Second Circuit precedents like Authors Guild and Swatch.

blogs.title: Fair Use at the Pleading Stage: Santos v. Kimmel as a Roadmap for 12(b)(6) Dismissals
blogs.description: Focusing on procedure, this post examines how the panel affirmed dismissal on fair use at Rule 12(b)(6), relying on the complaint, incorporated videos, and judicial notice of copyright registrations. It connects the approach to TCA Television and Cariou’s instruction that courts can decide fair use by comparing the works themselves. The piece assesses the strategic implications for media defendants and plaintiffs alike: when early motions are viable, what records matter, and how pleading choices can foreclose discovery in commentary and satire cases.

blogs.title: When Platform Terms Don’t Save You: Why Santos’s Contract and Fraud Theories Failed
blogs.description: This post analyzes the state-law rulings: (1) the direct breach claim failed because Santos wasn’t a third-party beneficiary of Cameo’s Terms under Illinois’s strong presumption against nonparty enforcement; (2) the implied-in-fact contract claim failed under New York law for not alleging essential terms or a meeting of the minds; and (3) the fraudulent inducement claim failed for lack of out-of-pocket loss. It explains why the panel sidestepped preemption and instead resolved the claims on their merits, and offers practical lessons for creators using platforms: if you want enforceable use restrictions, secure your own written terms and be able to plead concrete reliance losses.

blogs.title: Satire, Stings, and the Creator Economy: The Broader Stakes of Santos v. Kimmel for Cameo and Political Speech
blogs.description: Looking beyond the doctrinal holdings, this post explores how the decision normalizes satirical reuse of commissioned content obtained through ruses, so long as the secondary use offers commentary and doesn’t substitute for the original market. It considers what this means for celebrities and politicians monetizing personalized videos, the limits of platform-based restrictions, and the likely resilience of First Amendment–inflected fair use defenses for late-night shows and journalists. The piece closes with risk-management steps for creators and platforms in an era of pranks, political stings, and rapid content repurposing.
